questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix
questions.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition
questions.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{26}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
For the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/d19df62851eeb549464dd522cabcb4f5ab982ed4cdf39a81e6c18642299270f2.png) find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m \times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
\sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n \times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,{4}^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $A=U \Sigma V ^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T,
$$

where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$ 

First, notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14095495/assets/877912dffd62a0657f08fc4bc28158e1199daadbda3d92610a0c0f63055f5960.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
